title: CoraQuest - an adorable, family-weight dungeon crawl with a lot of charm
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZvUISEnjqbQ

Daniel (@dungeondive) looks at CoraQuest, designed by Cora and Dan Hughes — a father-and-daughter lockdown project turned Kickstarter darling, with Cora's original art tidied up by her dad. It sits squarely in HeroQuest territory: a family co-op for one to four players, ages six and up, ten standalone quests with names like Fangs for the Memory and The Great Teapot Caper, and a persistently troublesome gnome named Kevin.

The mechanism he genuinely admires is the timer. An exploration token sits on the tile stack; take a free action to reveal a new tile and it moves to your character card. End a round without exploring and the timer ticks. Run it out and spiders spawn on every web tile, then it resets to two. It never makes you lose — it just makes standing still expensive.

His criticisms are pointed. You always play four heroes regardless of player count, the same complaint he levels at Mice and Mystics. And too many turns pass where nothing interesting happens: the dice are stingy, the determination mechanic that grants an extra die after a miss rarely rescues anything, and a single unconscious hero can end the run. In an introductory game aimed at children, he wants far more ways to mitigate bad luck.

----

For a first dungeon crawl aimed at kids, how much should the design protect players from bad dice — or is learning to lose part of the lesson?
